## Fixed finite Gaussian derivative programs {#sec-mfp-finite-derivative-programs}

The conditioning identities above become an operational calculus once the
permitted finite computations and derivatives are specified. The order is to
differentiate the finite network, expand every represented matrix action,
and then evaluate a finite Gaussian expectation graph. The first two steps
are exact at finite width. The last step gives a width limit, including
convergence of expectations. Its scope is a fixed computation: depth,
derivative order and update count do not grow with width.

### Typed language and limit theorem {#sec-mfp-program-language}

::: {#def-mfp-primitive-program}
### Finite Gaussian program

A vector type labels one copy of $\mathbb R^n$. Fix finitely many types and
named initialized matrices $W:\mathbb R^n_\tau\to\mathbb R^n_\sigma$, with
$\tau\ne\sigma$. Each matrix has independent $N(0,1/n)$ entries, and different
named matrices are independent. A transpose call uses that same matrix.
For each type fix a finite Gaussian root tuple whose coordinate tuples are
iid over neuron indices. Its mean and covariance are fixed; its covariance
may be singular. Root tuples of distinct types and all matrices are
independent. A constant vector means a vector with one fixed scalar in every
coordinate, not an arbitrary width-dependent deterministic array.

A primitive program is a finite acyclic list of scalar and typed vector
instructions:

- **Coordinate map:** $v_i=F(u_i^1,\ldots,u_i^k;s_1,\ldots,s_b)$,
  with all vectors of the same type.
- **Normalized average:** $s=n^{-1}\sum_i F(u_i^1,\ldots,u_i^k;t_1,\ldots,t_b)$.
- **Scalar arithmetic:** sums and products of earlier scalars.
- **Named matrix action:** $Wh$ or $W^Tu$, with the declared input and output types.

Initial scalars are deterministic. Every $F$ is a finite expression made
from its arguments, fixed real constants, sums, products and
$\phi^{(r)}$, $r\ge0$, where

$$
\begin{aligned}
\phi&\in C^\infty(\mathbb R),\\
|\phi^{(r)}(x)|&\le C_r(1+|x|)^{d_r}
\quad\text{for every }r\ge0.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-activation-growth}

All coefficients, root laws, expression lists and dimensions other than
$n$ are fixed before $n\to\infty$. There is no coordinate selection,
inverse operation, arbitrary tensor-index contraction or width-dependent
coefficient primitive.
:::

A current matrix and a matrix direction may be stored, respectively, as

$$
A=W_0+\sum_{\nu=1}^M c_\nu u_\nu v_\nu^T/n,
\qquad B=\sum_{\nu=1}^{M'} d_\nu p_\nu q_\nu^T/n,
$$ {#eq-mfp-represented-matrices}

with a fixed finite number of terms; the initialized part may be absent.
These are notation for primitive actions, not extra random-matrix laws:

$$
\begin{aligned}
Ah&=W_0h+\sum_\nu c_\nu u_\nu(v_\nu^Th/n),\\
A^Tu&=W_0^Tu+\sum_\nu c_\nu v_\nu(u_\nu^Tu/n).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-rank-lowering}

Each pairing contracts only one type. The derivative language additionally
allows derivatives in finitely many deterministic inputs or scalar
parameters; fixed-order directional derivatives with program vector
directions and represented matrix directions; ambient gradients with
mobility $n$ on trainable vector roots and mobility one on trainable
matrices, with fixed block multipliers; their admitted contractions and
directional derivatives; fixed numbers of gradient updates; and finite
gradient-flow jets. The exact rules are in [exact finite differentiation](#sec-mfp-physical-differentiation).
No derivative of a sampling law is implicit in a parameter derivative.

::: {#thm-mfp-finite-derivative-program}
### Scalar limits and uniform moments

Every derivative program just specified expands exactly at each finite $n$
to a finite primitive program. The construction in [Gaussian source-response evaluation](#sec-mfp-source-evaluation)
gives a deterministic scalar $O_*$ for each scalar output $O_n$, and

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E|O_n-O_*|^p=0
\qquad(1\le p<\infty).
$$ {#eq-mfp-scalar-lp-limit}

For every vector node $v_n$, scalar node $s_n$, and finite $p,q\ge1$,

$$
\sup_n\mathbb E\left(\frac1n\sum_i|v_{n,i}|^p\right)^q<\infty,
\qquad \sup_n\mathbb E|s_n|^q<\infty.
$$ {#eq-mfp-uniform-node-moments}

Every same-type tuple of vector nodes has a deterministic joint empirical
law converging in probability in $\mathcal W_2$, for the Euclidean metric
on the tuple. Its law is the source-response law below. These assertions
hold jointly for finitely many programs sharing roots and matrices,
including singular query Grams.

The theorem asserts no infinite Taylor-series convergence, positive-time
reconstruction, common existence horizon for finite flows, growing-depth
or growing-update limit, or bound on compilation complexity beyond
finiteness. Vector coordinates do not converge to deterministic constants.
:::

The proof has three parts. A raw-entry differentiation estimate bounds all
moments without rank assumptions. The established bounded-derivative
Gaussian program law identifies each clipped program; the moment bounds
remove clipping uniformly in width. Exact finite differentiation closes
the language before this probabilistic argument is applied.

### Gaussian source-response evaluation {#sec-mfp-source-evaluation}

Give each type $\tau$ a probability space $\Omega_\tau$ and expectation
$\mathbb E_\tau$. Capital letters denote scalar representatives of vector
nodes. Roots have their declared laws; coordinate maps act on these
representatives and on previously computed deterministic scalars. An
average becomes the expectation on its type.

For a named matrix $W:\tau\to\sigma$, list forward calls $y_r=Wh_r$
and reverse calls $v_s=W^Tu_s$ in their program order. Their scalar inputs
are $H_r$ on $\Omega_\tau$ and $U_s$ on $\Omega_\sigma$. Introduce centered
Gaussian sources $\xi_r$ on the output type $\sigma$, and $\zeta_s$ on
the output type $\tau$, with

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(\xi_r,\xi_t)=\mathbb E_\tau[H_rH_t],\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\zeta_s,\zeta_v)=\mathbb E_\sigma[U_sU_v].
$$ {#eq-mfp-source-grams}

Different oriented matrix groups, including the two orientations of one
matrix, are independent Gaussian groups and are independent of the roots.
Return

$$
\begin{aligned}
Y_r&=\xi_r+\sum_{s:\,\text{earlier reverse call}}
 U_s\,\mathbb E_\tau[\partial_{\zeta_s}H_r],\\
V_s&=\zeta_s+\sum_{r:\,\text{earlier forward call}}
 H_r\,\mathbb E_\sigma[\partial_{\xi_r}U_s].
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-source-response}

The source covariances use uncentered input second moments. Thus an input
$H=1$ has source variance one. The independence assertion concerns sources;
the output fields in @eq-mfp-source-response generally depend on earlier
groups through their responses.

A formal source partial differentiates the explicit expression in the
named source arguments, holding all previously computed expectations,
covariance entries and scalar coefficients fixed. Paths through other
matrices' earlier calls remain part of that expression. An unavailable
source has derivative zero. Each call retains a distinct formal argument
even at singular covariance: compute partials before restricting to the
Gaussian support. No covariance inverse is an evaluation rule.

This is a causal construction. Every response integrand is already
defined, and the next covariance is an input-Gram extension, hence positive
semidefinite. A Gaussian law exists even when that extension is singular.
Finite sums, products, composition and differentiation preserve polynomial
growth of every derivative, by the finite product and chain rules.
Induction therefore bounds every field and its formal derivatives by a
polynomial in the finite root/source list, so all required expectations
exist. Collecting them gives a finite directed acyclic graph

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_j&=\int F_j(g;I_1,\ldots,I_{j-1})\\
&\qquad N(0,K_j(I_1,\ldots,I_{j-1}))(dg),\\
O_*&=P(I_1,\ldots,I_N),
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-expectation-graph}

where root means are fixed shifts inside $F_j$. The final $P$ is a
polynomial because scalar outputs are assembled from averages, sums and
products. The dimensions, integrands and covariance entries are specified
by the program, rather than supplied as unknown neural laws.

### Uniform raw-entry moments {#sec-mfp-uniform-moments}

The following finite-entry cancellation argument is adapted from the
moment mechanism in Appendix J of @golikov2022nongaussian. Its needed form
is proved here; no external program theorem is used as a hypothesis.

::: {#lem-mfp-raw-entry-moments}
### Moments of values and raw-entry derivatives

Temporarily allow all independent centered Gaussian matrix entries to
have different variances, each at most $1/n$. For a fixed primitive
program with smooth maps whose every partial derivative has polynomial
growth, let $\alpha$ be a list of $k$ raw matrix-entry differentiation
variables, with repetition allowed. For each finite $p\ge1$ and $k\ge0$,

$$
\sup_{n,i,|\alpha|=k}\mathbb E|\partial^\alpha v_{n,i}|^p<\infty,
\qquad
\sup_{n,|\alpha|=k}\mathbb E|\partial^\alpha s_n|^p<\infty.
$$ {#eq-mfp-raw-entry-bounds}

Constants are uniform over these variances and depend only on the fixed
graph, root laws and finitely many polynomial derivative bounds. They
are consequently uniform over any family of maps having common such
bounds at each order. Derivatives refer to the deterministic program as
a function of unconstrained raw entries, evaluated at the random array;
this includes entries of variance zero.
:::

[]{#proof-mfp-raw-entry-moments}

::: {.proof}
Induct over instructions, proving all finite moments and derivative orders
simultaneously at each node. At fixed $n$, values and derivatives have
polynomial growth in finitely many Gaussian variables, so integrability
is available before uniform bounds are proved. Roots have Gaussian moments
and positive-order matrix derivatives zero. Repeated product and chain
rules for coordinate and scalar maps give finitely many products of earlier
derivatives and polynomially bounded factors. Hölder's inequality and
higher moments of the earlier nodes bound each term. This covers scalar
feedback. For an average, differentiate its finite sum and use

$$
\mathbb E\left|\frac1n\sum_i a_i\right|^p
\le\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E|a_i|^p.
$$ {#eq-mfp-average-jensen}

For a matrix call $y=Wv$, the product rule gives

$$
\partial^\alpha y_i=\sum_jW_{ij}\partial^\alpha v_j+R_i.
$$ {#eq-mfp-matrix-derivative}

The remainder has at most $k$ terms, each an earlier-node derivative of
order $k-1$: differentiating the linear matrix factor fixes its column
index, and a second derivative of that factor vanishes. Thus $R_i$ is
bounded. A transpose call has the same argument with a column in place
of a row.

Write $w_j=W_{ij}$ and $z_j=\partial^\alpha v_j$. It suffices to bound
an even integer moment $p$ of $\sum_jw_jz_j$, since larger even moments
bound every finite moment. Expand it into ordered tuples
$(j_1,\ldots,j_p)$. For one tuple let $b$ be its number of distinct
indices, let $S$ be the indices that appear exactly once, and put
$s=|S|$, $M=\prod_{a=1}^p w_{j_a}$ and $Z=\prod_{a=1}^p z_{j_a}$.
We will bound $|\mathbb E[MZ]|$ by $C n^{-b}$.

For $u\in S$ define the commuting difference
$\Delta_uZ=Z-Z|_{w_u=0}$. Centering and independence give
$\mathbb E[MZ]=\mathbb E[M\prod_{u\in S}\Delta_u Z]$:
in every other term of the expanded product at least one singleton
weight appears only as its centered linear factor. Applying the
fundamental theorem of calculus once in each such entry yields

$$
\mathbb E[MZ]=\int_{[0,1]^s}
\mathbb E\left[M\prod_{u\in S}w_u\,
 (\partial_S Z)(W^{(t)})\right]dt.
$$ {#eq-mfp-singleton-cancellation}

Here $W^{(t)}$ replaces each selected raw entry $w_u$ by $t_uw_u$
in the entire array, consistently in every reuse and transpose. Empty
products and a zero-dimensional integral cover $s=0$. Gaussian moments
give

$$
\mathbb E\left|M\prod_{u\in S}w_u\right|^2
\le C n^{-(p+s)}.
$$

The other factor in @eq-mfp-singleton-cancellation has a bounded second
moment, uniformly in $n,t$ and the selected entries. Its product-rule
expansion contains only derivatives of the earlier node $v$, evaluated
at independent centered Gaussian entries of variances at most $1/n$.
The strengthened induction hypothesis applies. Differentiate in raw
coordinates first and then evaluate at $W^{(t)}$; these are not
derivatives of the composed map $W\mapsto Z(W^{(t)})$. No factors
$t_u$ or divisions by $t_u$ occur, even at zero. Fixed-width polynomial
integrability justifies the centering and integration exchanges.

Cauchy--Schwarz bounds the tuple contribution by
$C n^{-(p+s)/2}$. The multiplicities satisfy
$p\ge s+2(b-s)=2b-s$, giving the desired $C n^{-b}$.
For a fixed equality pattern there are at most $C_p n^b$ tuples,
and finitely many patterns for fixed $p$. Summing proves a uniform
bound for the matrix-call moment and closes the induction. Every bound
uses finitely many earlier derivative bounds and Gaussian moments,
never a lower variance or a Gram inverse.
:::

Taking $k=0$ proves scalar moment bounds, and Jensen gives

$$
\mathbb E\left(\frac1n\sum_i|v_i|^p\right)^q
\le\frac1n\sum_i\mathbb E|v_i|^{pq},
$$

which proves @eq-mfp-uniform-node-moments. We also use the uniform
operator-norm moments from @eq-docs-special-data-limits-l3859 and
@eq-docs-special-data-limits-l3866: for every fixed finite $a$,
$\sup_n\mathbb E\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}^a<\infty$. Those estimates follow
from a $1/4$-net and Gaussian tails and apply to any fixed list of
initialized matrices and their transposes.

### Bounded maps, scalar feedback and removal of clipping {#sec-mfp-clipping-proof}

::: {#lem-mfp-bounded-typed-extension}
### The bounded-derivative foundation on a finite typed graph

For any fixed list of named matrices between distinct types, the source
rule @eq-mfp-source-response identifies empirical laws in $\mathcal W_2$
in probability for $C^1$ coordinate maps with bounded continuous first
partials. Normalized averages of such maps, globally Lipschitz scalar
maps, and globally Lipschitz dependence on preceding scalars are allowed.
The roots here may have any iid finite-second-moment tuple law of the
stated independence types.
:::

[]{#proof-mfp-bounded-typed-extension}

::: {.proof}
The deterministic-coefficient proof is
@thm-docs-special-data-limits-l3820, with adaptive conditioning in
[adaptive Gaussian conditioning](12-three-sample-learning.qmd#sec-docs-special-data-limits-l3884), the source identity in
@lem-docs-special-data-limits-l3966 and singular-query removal in
@lem-docs-special-data-limits-l4011. Its statement lists adjacent-layer
matrices. The following checks extend the proof to the present finite
typed graph without enlarging its analytic hypotheses.

Condition on all revealed roots and the complete preceding transcript.
For each *named* matrix retain only its own forward and reverse
constraints $WV=Y$, $W^TU=Q$. Initially the residual matrix laws are
independent Gaussians. A coordinate or scalar instruction is measurable
from the transcript. At the next call its input is fixed conditionally,
so its answer conditions only the queried residual matrix factor by one
linear observation; all other conditional factors are unchanged. This
proves by induction the conditional product structure used in
@eq-docs-special-data-limits-l3896 for any list of names, including
parallel edges and type-graph cycles. Chronology is still acyclic.

That conditioning formula and its new-query form
@eq-docs-special-data-limits-l3916 use only the two endpoint spaces and
their earlier query columns. The finite-rank projection error is
$\operatorname{rank}(U)/n$, regardless of other edges. Thus the
positive-Gram empirical-law induction, including its conditional test
variance and second-moment calculation, carries over verbatim at each
named call. The Gaussian integration-by-parts cancellation in
@lem-docs-special-data-limits-l3966 also uses only this matrix's two
lists. Dependencies through other matrices are retained in the input's
explicit source expression. This gives @eq-mfp-source-response with
separate oriented groups for every name.

For singular Grams, add a distinct independent $\varepsilon$-Gaussian
input perturbation at each call, as in
@lem-docs-special-data-limits-l4011. Each new squared distance to its
own preceding query span has limit at least $\varepsilon^2$.
A finite union of the operator-bound events controls all named matrices;
the same finite instruction induction gives an $O(\varepsilon)$ RMS
error. The proof's coupling by positive semidefinite covariance square
roots and its convergence of bounded source derivatives do not use
layer adjacency. It therefore removes $\varepsilon$ for this graph.

To include scalars, proceed causally, replacing each preceding scalar
value by its deterministic limit in an auxiliary program. A normalized
average of a bounded-derivative map is the normalized pairing of its
output with the constant-one vector, so the empirical $\mathcal W_2$
law determines that scalar limit. Globally Lipschitz scalar operations
preserve convergence. If $s_n\to s_*$ and $F(u;s)$ has a global
Lipschitz constant $C$, then

$$
\begin{gathered}
\frac{\|F(u_n;s_n)-F(\bar u_n;s_*)\|_2}{\sqrt n}\\
{}\le C\left(\sum_j\frac{\|u_n^j-\bar u_n^j\|_2}{\sqrt n}\right.\\
\left.{}+\sum_b|s_{n,b}-s_{*,b}|\right).
\end{gathered}
$$

For averages, Jensen gives the same estimate for their absolute error.
Matrix errors are bounded by the initialized operator norm times the
input RMS error. This proves the scalar and vector comparison by finite
induction; equivalently, scalar arguments can be broadcast and then
inserted into an ordinary same-type coordinate map. It is the mechanism
of [causal scalar feedback](12-three-sample-learning.qmd#sec-docs-special-data-limits-l4054) with this additional globally
Lipschitz coordinate dependence checked explicitly. The deterministic
scalar construction is causal, not a fixed-point assumption. In its
source partials the substituted scalars are held fixed. The same
Lipschitz estimates also include scalars when removing the singular-query
perturbations. This proves the stated extension.
:::

This lemma leaves intact the broader finite-second-moment roots and
$C^1$ hypotheses of the older foundation. The smooth Gaussian theorem
adds all finite scalar moments under its stronger assumptions; it does
not replace the lower-regularity specializations in
[contained probability and continuity specializations](#sec-docs-global-nonlinear-l1840) or the distinct feature-ascent theorem
@thm-docs-gaussian-calculus-l289.

[]{#proof-mfp-finite-derivative-program}

::: {.proof}
First consider a primitive program. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi$ equal
to one on the unit ball and zero outside the radius-two ball. For every
coordinate or scalar operation set
$F_B(x)=\chi(x/B)F(x)$, $B\ge1$, including scalar arguments in $x$.
Scalar sums and products can be clipped by this rule too; constants
are unchanged. Each $F_B$ has bounded derivatives and is globally
Lipschitz. For each derivative order its polynomial growth bound is
uniform in $B$: product-rule factors $B^{-j}D^j\chi(x/B)$ are
uniformly bounded. Also $F_B\to F$ with all derivatives on compact
sets. The raw-entry moment lemma consequently holds uniformly in both
$n$ and $B$ for the original and clipped programs.

Couple them using identical roots and matrices. We claim for corresponding
nodes that

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{B\to\infty}\sup_n\mathbb E\frac{\|v_n-v_n^B\|_2^2}{n}&=0,\\
\lim_{B\to\infty}\sup_n\mathbb E|s_n-s_n^B|^2&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-clipping-errors}

Here are the error estimates needed to induct over the list. Regard a
vector coordinate as a random variable on the original probability
space times the uniform distribution on its neuron index. All finite
moments are uniformly bounded on this probability space. If a difference
vanishes in $L^2$, interpolation with a uniformly bounded higher moment
makes it vanish in every fixed finite $L^p$, uniformly in width. This
also applies to scalar errors and scalar broadcasts.

Polynomial growth of first derivatives gives

$$
|F(x)-F(y)|\le C(1+|x|+|y|)^d|x-y|.
$$ {#eq-mfp-polynomial-difference}

Split $F(x)-F_B(y)$ into $F(x)-F(y)$ and $F(y)-F_B(y)$.
The first tends to zero in $L^2$ by Hölder, the input errors upgraded
to $L^4$, and uniform moments of the polynomial factor. The second
is bounded by $C(1+|y|)^d\mathbf1_{|y|>B}$. Its squared expectation
vanishes uniformly by any sufficiently high moment and a power tail
bound. This proves the coordinate, scalar and, by Jensen, average steps.

For a matrix call with input error $e$, correlated with $W$ or not,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E\frac{\|We\|_2^2}{n}
&\le (\mathbb E\|W\|_{\mathrm{op}}^4)^{1/2}
 \left[\mathbb E(\|e\|_2^2/n)^2\right]^{1/2}\\
&\le C\left[\mathbb E\frac1n\sum_i|e_i|^4\right]^{1/2}
\longrightarrow0.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-correlated-matrix-error}

The operator moments and the interpolation just proved justify the last
line. Transposes obey the identical bound, and roots have zero error.
This completes the induction proving @eq-mfp-clipping-errors, including
causal scalar feedback.

For fixed $B$, @lem-mfp-bounded-typed-extension identifies the clipped
program and gives $O_n^B\to O_*^B$ in probability. The clipped Gaussian
evaluator converges to the unclipped evaluator. To prove this, induct
over its expectation graph. Earlier convergent coefficients stay bounded.
All fields and each finite set of source derivatives have common
polynomial bounds in the finite root/source list, because the clipped
maps have common derivative bounds of polynomial growth. Couple each
source prefix with a fixed standard Gaussian vector using its positive
semidefinite covariance square root. Covariance convergence implies
square-root convergence, including at rank loss, by the argument in
@lem-docs-special-data-limits-l4011. Local convergence of the maps and
their derivatives gives pointwise convergence on this coupling; bounded
square roots give a common polynomial Gaussian dominator. Dominated
convergence therefore passes input Grams, response expectations and
all fixed field moments to their unclipped values. This closes the
coefficient induction and proves $O_*^B\to O_*$.

For any $\epsilon>0$ and sufficiently large fixed $B$,

$$
\Pr(|O_n-O_*|>\epsilon)
\le\Pr(|O_n-O_n^B|>\epsilon/3)
   +\Pr(|O_n^B-O_*^B|>\epsilon/3).
$$

Take the width limit and then $B\to\infty$, using
@eq-mfp-clipping-errors and Markov's inequality. This proves convergence
in probability. For finite $p$, choose $q>p$. The raw-entry moment
bound controls $\mathbb E|O_n-O_*|^q$ uniformly. The part of its $p$th
moment on $|O_n-O_*|>R$ is at most $CR^{p-q}$; the part on the
complement tends to zero by convergence in probability and boundedness
(split once more at an arbitrarily small threshold). This proves
@eq-mfp-scalar-lp-limit.

For a same-type vector tuple, the coordinatewise coupling bounds the
squared empirical $\mathcal W_2$ distance by its mean squared error.
The clipped empirical laws converge by the bounded lemma, and their
limiting laws converge in $\mathcal W_2$ by the Gaussian dominated
convergence just proved. The triangle inequality proves the asserted
unclipped empirical-law convergence in probability. Finite unions of
programs give the joint assertions. Finally,
@prp-mfp-derivative-closure below expands every admitted derivative to
a primitive graph before clipping; thus this proof applies to the
actual derivative, never to a derivative of a clipped network.
:::

### Exact finite differentiation and training {#sec-mfp-physical-differentiation}

Physical differentiation acts on the realized finite-dimensional program,
then evaluates at sampled parameters. A single Fréchet derivative evaluates
its direction at the base point and holds that direction fixed. With
$\delta u=Du[\delta\theta]$ and $\delta s=Ds[\delta\theta]$, its rules are

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta F(u;s)
&=\sum_j F_{u^j}(u;s)\odot\delta u^j\\
&\quad+\sum_b F_{s_b}(u;s)\,\delta s_b,\\
\delta\left[\frac1n\sum_iF(u_i;s)\right]
&=\frac1n\sum_i\bigl[\sum_jF_{u^j}(u_i;s)\delta u_i^j\\
&\qquad+\sum_bF_{s_b}(u_i;s)\delta s_b\bigr],\\
\delta(Ah)&=(\delta A)h+A\delta h,\\
\delta(A^Tu)&=(\delta A)^Tu+A^T\delta u,\\
\delta(cuv^T/n)&=(\delta c)uv^T/n\\
&\quad+c(\delta u)v^T/n\\
&\quad+cu(\delta v)^T/n.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-forward-ad}

Products of vectors in these expressions are coordinatewise. Scalar
arithmetic uses the usual sum and product rules. Unlike a formal source
partial, physical differentiation propagates through finite averages
and their scalar feedback.

For reverse differentiation of a scalar $O$, store vector adjoints
$b_u=n\,\partial O/\partial u$ and scalar adjoints
$a_s=\partial O/\partial s$. Initialize $a_O=1$ and the others at zero;
visit instructions in reverse order and add every contribution:

For a coordinate map $v=F(u;s)$, add for each argument

$$
b_{u^j}\mathrel{+}=b_v\odot F_{u^j},\qquad
a_{s_b}\mathrel{+}=\frac1n\sum_i b_{v,i}F_{s_b}(u_i;s).
$$ {#eq-mfp-coordinate-adjoint}

For an average $t=n^{-1}\sum_iF(u_i;s)$, add

$$
b_{u^j}\mathrel{+}=a_tF_{u^j},\qquad
a_{s_b}\mathrel{+}=\frac{a_t}{n}\sum_iF_{s_b}(u_i;s).
$$ {#eq-mfp-average-adjoint}

For a matrix action $v=Au$, add

$$
b_u\mathrel{+}=A^Tb_v,\qquad \nabla_AO\mathrel{+}=b_vu^T/n.
$$ {#eq-mfp-matrix-adjoint}

For a transpose action $v=A^Tu$, add

$$
b_u\mathrel{+}=Ab_v,\qquad \nabla_AO\mathrel{+}=ub_v^T/n.
$$ {#eq-mfp-transpose-adjoint}

For example, matching $dO=b_v^Tdv/n$ to
$\langle\nabla_AO,dA\rangle_F+b_u^Tdu/n$ proves both matrix rules,
where $\langle B,C\rangle_F=\operatorname{tr}(B^TC)$.
Accumulation includes every repeated occurrence of a shared parameter.

Compute a current ambient-matrix gradient with $A$ treated as the
parameter *before* substituting @eq-mfp-represented-matrices. A derivative
with respect to the factors of previous updates is a history pullback,
a different requested function. Vector mobility $n\kappa$ gives loss
velocity $-\kappa b_u$, and matrix mobility $\kappa$ gives
$-\kappa\nabla_A\mathcal L$. Their contractions stay in the language:

$$
\begin{aligned}
n\,\nabla_uO^T\nabla_uS
&=\frac{(b_u^O)^Tb_u^S}{n},\\
\left\langle\frac{uv^T}{n},\frac{pq^T}{n}\right\rangle_F
&=\left(\frac{u^Tp}{n}\right)\left(\frac{v^Tq}{n}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-gradient-contractions}

For physical-time jets write
$u_{[r]}=\frac1{r!}(d^ru/dt^r)(0)$. At a fixed requested order $R$,
coefficient extraction in the truncated polynomial ring gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
(uv)_{[r]}&=\sum_{a+b=r}u_{[a]}v_{[b]},\qquad
(Au)_{[r]}=\sum_{a+b=r}A_{[a]}u_{[b]},\\
\phi(u)_{[r]}&=[t^r]\sum_{k=0}^r\frac{\phi^{(k)}(u_{[0]})}{k!}
                 \left(\sum_{j=1}^r u_{[j]}t^j\right)^k.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-jet-algebra}

The $k=0$ term is the constant $\phi(u_{[0]})$. Averages act
coefficientwise, and mixed finite jets use multivariate truncated
polynomials. For a smooth finite-dimensional field
$\dot\theta=V(\theta)$, compute

$$
(r+1)\theta_{[r+1]}=[t^r]V\left(\sum_{j=0}^r\theta_{[j]}t^j\right).
$$ {#eq-mfp-flow-jet-recursion}

All state dependence in $V$ participates. In particular
$O''=D^2O[V,V]+DO[DV[V]]$; the first term alone describes the straight
line with frozen initial direction. This is the general version of
[derivatives along the gradient direction](#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l170) and the explicit finite MLP recurrence
in [the finite MLP jet recurrence](#sec-docs-gaussian-calculus-l5338).

::: {#prp-mfp-derivative-closure}
### Exact compilation of admitted derivatives

The derivative constructions above, fixed gradient updates and fixed-order
flow jets expand to primitive programs, exactly at every finite width.
:::

[]{#proof-mfp-derivative-closure}

::: {.proof}
Every partial derivative of an allowed coordinate expression is again
such an expression by finite chain and product rules. Thus
@eq-mfp-forward-ad and the reverse table introduce only allowed coordinate
maps, averages and matrix actions. Differentiating a represented matrix
term leaves finitely many represented terms; @eq-mfp-rank-lowering expands
their actions, and @eq-mfp-gradient-contractions expands their admitted
contractions. A vector update subtracts a program vector, while a matrix
update adds finitely many normalized rank-one terms. Induction over a fixed
number of simultaneous steps proves exact closure, with the ambient loss
gradient formed before each current-state substitution.

Finite Taylor's theorem, not analyticity, proves
@eq-mfp-jet-algebra to any prescribed finite order. Comparing coefficients
in $\dot\theta=V(\theta)$ gives @eq-mfp-flow-jet-recursion. A smooth
finite-dimensional field has a local solution: on a sufficiently small
closed ball its derivative is bounded, and its integral map on continuous
paths in that ball is a contraction for sufficiently short time. Repeated
differentiation yields the finite jets. No common width-independent
interval is used. Finite induction on jet order therefore proves the
remaining closure assertion. Applying the limit theorem only after
expansion avoids any interchange of differentiation and the width limit.
:::

Explicitly frozen direction data can be handled as independent seeds on
an enlarged parameter space, with values assigned from the base state
after differentiation. For example, freezing $x$ inside $n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^2$
sets its partial derivative in the remaining $x$ parameter to zero;
it is no longer the ordinary derivative of the original observable.
Gaussian evaluation retains the seed's value and explicit source
dependence. Freezing physical seeds never freezes a formal source path.

For neural applications fix $L,m,d$ and the canonical forward model

$$
\begin{aligned}
z_a^{(1)}&=W^{(1)}x_a/\sqrt d,\\
z_a^{(\ell)}&=W^{(\ell)}h_a^{(\ell-1)},\\
h_a^{(\ell)}&=\phi(z_a^{(\ell)}),\\
f_{n,a}&=(W^{(L+1)})^Th_a^{(L)}/n.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-neural-forward}

Take independent first-weight entries $N(0,1)$, hidden entries $N(0,1/n)$,
and stored readout entries $N(0,\tau^2)$ for a fixed $\tau$.
The first-matrix columns and readout are vector roots. This is an
order-one readout when $\tau>0$, explicitly distinct from the default
width-dependent small-readout law in [the notation contract](notation.qmd#sec-docs-notation-l70). With
$r_{n,a}=f_{n,a}-y_a$, full mean loss
$\mathcal L_n=m^{-1}\sum_a r_{n,a}^2$, and block mobilities
$n\kappa_1,\kappa_2,\ldots,\kappa_L,n\kappa_{L+1}$, its physical
gradient field is admitted. All samples share the first-matrix columns;
one must not replace correlated sample preactivations by independent
trainable parameters. Fixed data derivatives also propagate through those
shared columns. Exact small-readout finite recurrences remain valid,
but their width-dependent initialization is not a consequence of this
fixed-root-law theorem.

### Initialization activation-moment form {#sec-mfp-initialization-normal-form}

::: {#prp-mfp-initialization-normal-form}
### Restricted activation-moment reduction

Construct the original feedforward preactivations of the centered,
zero-bias initialization in @eq-mfp-neural-forward first. Consider a
compiled derivative program at
initialization in which every nonlinear node is literally
$\phi^{(r)}(z_a^{(\ell)}(0))$ for one of these original nodes. All other
operations are the allowed polynomial arithmetic, matrix actions and
normalized contractions. Its scalar limit is a finite polynomial in fixed
model/data constants and recursively computed Gaussian moments of products
of activation derivatives. This syntactic restriction excludes nonlinear
functions of derivative fields and of updated preactivations.
:::

[]{#proof-mfp-initialization-normal-form}

::: {.proof}
No reverse call precedes the original forward pass. Hence its preactivations
are centered Gaussian sources, or linear combinations of first-layer
Gaussian roots. Their covariances are determined in order by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Sigma^{(1)}_{ab}&=G_{ab}=x_a^Tx_b/d,\\
\Sigma^{(\ell+1)}_{ab}
&=\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,\Sigma^{(\ell)})}\phi(Z_a)\phi(Z_b).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-forward-covariances}

All original preactivations, auxiliary roots and later named sources form
a finite joint Gaussian family on each type. A preactivation represented
as a linear combination can be adjoined as a Gaussian integration
coordinate with its induced covariance, even if this creates singularity.
Source partials still use the original named arguments; adjoining an
integration coordinate does not change their definition.

Inductively every field is a finite sum of expressions
$cP(Z)\prod_\nu\phi^{(r_\nu)}(Z_{a_\nu})$, with $P$ polynomial,
activation arguments designated original preactivations, and $c$
polynomial in previously computed scalar values. Fixed means of auxiliary
roots can be absorbed into the polynomial; designated activation arguments
are centered preactivations by the subclass assumption. The class is closed under arithmetic
and formal source derivatives. A matrix action appends one Gaussian
source and linear combinations of old fields with coefficients equal
to expectations in the same class; its covariance entries are also
such expectations. This proves the symbolic induction.

For any centered Gaussian vector $Z$ of covariance $K$ and smooth
polynomial-growth $F$,

$$
\mathbb E[Z_iF(Z)]=\sum_jK_{ij}\mathbb E[\partial_jF(Z)].
$$ {#eq-mfp-stein-reduction}

Indeed write $Z=B\gamma$, $BB^T=K$, with independent standard Gaussian
coordinates in $\gamma$, and integrate by parts in each coordinate.
Polynomial growth removes boundary terms and justifies Fubini; no
invertibility is needed. Apply this identity to one explicit Gaussian
factor in $P$. A derivative hitting the remaining polynomial reduces
its degree, and a derivative hitting an activation raises its derivative
order while still removing the selected explicit Gaussian factor.
Induction on polynomial degree terminates in covariance monomials times
atoms

$$
\mathbb E_{Z\sim N(0,K_j)}\prod_\nu\phi^{(r_{j,\nu})}(Z_{a_{j,\nu}}),
$$

whose covariances are already determined by earlier steps. Substituting
these finite expressions recursively proves the claimed polynomial form.
For polynomial-only programs this reduces to
@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l211. The scalar $L^p$ theorem identifies the
result with the expectation limit; the reduction is not a separate
asymptotic assumption.
:::

### Worked programs and neural observables {#sec-mfp-worked-programs}

**Reuse and the finite-width correction.** Let $e$ be the constant-one
input, $y=We$, $u=\phi(y)$, $v=W^Tu$ and $J_n=v^Tv/n$.
For a standard Gaussian $\gamma$, put
$q=\mathbb E\phi(\gamma)^2$ and $c=\mathbb E\phi'(\gamma)$.
The forward representative is $\xi\sim N(0,1)$; the reverse one is
$\zeta+c$ with $\zeta\sim N(0,q)$. Thus

$$
\begin{aligned}
J_n&\longrightarrow q+c^2\quad\text{in every finite }L^p,\\
\mathbb E J_n&=q+c^2\\
&\quad+\frac{\mathbb E[\gamma^2\phi(\gamma)^2]-q-c^2}{n}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-reuse-square}

For the finite identity, use the exact projection law
@eq-docs-gaussian-calculus-l34: conditionally on $y$ the two orthogonal
components of $v$ give
$\mathbb E[J_n\mid y]=(n^{-1}y^T\phi(y))^2+
(1-1/n)n^{-1}\|\phi(y)\|_2^2$. Taking expectations and using
$\mathbb E[\gamma\phi(\gamma)]=c$ proves the formula. For $\phi(x)=x$
it gives $2+1/n$, whereas Gaussian compilation returns $2$.
Physical differentiation must accumulate both occurrences of $W$:

$$
\nabla_WJ_n=\frac2n\left[
uv^T+\bigl((Wv)\odot\phi'(y)\bigr)e^T\right].
$$

This follows by substituting
$dv=(dW)^Tu+W^T(\phi'(y)\odot(dW)e)$ into $dJ_n=2v^Tdv/n$.

**One normalized update.** For the explicitly different scalar loss
$\mathcal L_n=n^{-1}\sum_i\phi((We)_i)$, set $p=\phi'(We)$.
The differential gives $\nabla_W\mathcal L_n=pe^T/n$. One step with
fixed $\eta$ and matrix mobility one gives $A=W-\eta pe^T/n$.
Keep $p$ at its pre-update value. Exact lowering yields
$A^Tp=W^Tp-\eta e(p^Tp/n)$ and $Ae=We-\eta p$. With
$q=\mathbb E\phi'(\gamma)^2$ and $c=\mathbb E\phi''(\gamma)$,

$$
\frac{\|A^Tp\|_2^2}{n}\longrightarrow q+(c-\eta q)^2.
$$

The reverse source has variance $q$ and response $c$, while the saved
pairing tends to $q$; this proves the formula. For $\phi(x)=x^4/4$
the answer is $15+(3-15\eta)^2$.

**Singular duplicate calls.** Distinct calls $y_1=We$, $y_2=We$
retain sources of covariance $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$.
For $u=\phi(y_1+y_2)$ the two formal partials are separately
$\phi'(\xi_1+\xi_2)$. On the Gaussian support
$(\xi_1,\xi_2)=(\gamma,\gamma)$, so

$$
\frac{\|W^Tu\|_2^2}{n}\longrightarrow
\mathbb E\phi(2\gamma)^2+4(\mathbb E\phi'(2\gamma))^2.
$$

This also follows by applying @eq-mfp-reuse-square to $\phi(2x)$.
For $u=\phi(y_1)-\phi(y_2)$ the source variance is zero and the
two response coefficients cancel. Its transpose output remains exactly
zero. Identifying the formal arguments before differentiation would
discard the information that makes this cancellation explicit.

**Moving direction.** Let $x\in\mathbb R^n$ be a trainable vector
state, not a dataset input, with iid standard Gaussian initialization.
For $\mathcal L_n=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^4/4$ and vector mobility $n$,
$\dot x=-x^3$. The observable $O_n=n^{-1}\sum_i x_i^2$ satisfies

$$
D^2O_n[V,V]=\frac2n\sum_i x_i^6,\qquad
DO_n[DV[V]]=\frac6n\sum_i x_i^6.
$$

The expected initial frozen and moving second derivatives therefore tend
to $30$ and $120$. The moving coefficient $O_{[2]}$ tends to $60$,
because jets include $1/2!$. Directly,
$x_i(t)=x_i(0)(1+2t x_i(0)^2)^{-1/2}$ verifies these finite identities.

**A neural parameter derivative.** Take two hidden layers, scalar input
$x=1$, no biases, and independent
$W_i^{(1)},W_i^{(3)}\sim N(0,1)$,
$W_{ij}^{(2)}\sim N(0,1/n)$. This explicitly uses order-one readout.
The forward pass is @eq-mfp-neural-forward, with
$z^{(1)}=W^{(1)}$. Define
$b^{(1)}=n\nabla_{W^{(1)}}f_n$ and
$O_n=\|b^{(1)}\|_2^2/n=n\|\nabla_{W^{(1)}}f_n\|_2^2$.
Compute in order

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_1&=\mathbb E\phi(\gamma)^2,\\
Z&\sim N(0,q_1),\\
s_1&=\mathbb E\phi'(\gamma)^2,\\
s_2&=\mathbb E\phi'(Z)^2,\\
q_2&=\mathbb E\phi(Z)^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

Then $O_n\to s_1s_2$ in every finite $L^p$. Indeed exact differentiation
gives $\delta^{(2)}=W^{(3)}\odot\phi'(z^{(2)})$ and
$b^{(1)}=\phi'(z^{(1)})\odot W^{(2)T}\delta^{(2)}$.
The transpose response is $\mathbb E[A\phi''(Z)]=0$, since the
centered readout representative $A$ is independent of $Z$. Its reverse
source has variance $s_2$ and is independent of the first-layer root;
the squared product consequently has expectation $s_1s_2$. Likewise
the full metric gradient norm tends to

$$
n\|\nabla_{W^{(1)}}f_n\|_2^2+
\|\nabla_{W^{(2)}}f_n\|_F^2+
n\|\nabla_{W^{(3)}}f_n\|_2^2
\longrightarrow s_1s_2+q_1s_2+q_2,
$$

using $\nabla_{W^{(2)}}f_n=\delta^{(2)}h^{(1)T}/n$ and
$n\nabla_{W^{(3)}}f_n=h^{(2)}$.

**Symbolic geometry and feature-kernel jets.** Keep two hidden layers and
order-one readout, now with $m=d=2$. Fix real
$\alpha,\beta,\gamma,y_1,y_2$ and set

$$
x_1/\sqrt2=(\alpha,0)^T,\quad
x_2/\sqrt2=(\beta,\gamma)^T,\qquad
G=\begin{pmatrix}\alpha^2&\alpha\beta\\
\alpha\beta&\beta^2+\gamma^2\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Let $U,V$ be the shared columns of $W^{(1)}$, each with iid $N(0,1)$
entries, so $z_1^{(1)}=\alpha U$ and
$z_2^{(1)}=\beta U+\gamma V$. With the forward pass above, use
the half-mean loss and its physical clock

$$
\begin{gathered}
\mathcal L_n=\frac1{2m}\sum_a(f_{n,a}-y_a)^2,\\
(\dot U,\dot V,\dot W^{(2)},\dot W^{(3)})\\
=-\bigl(n\nabla_U\mathcal L_n,n\nabla_V\mathcal L_n,\\
\qquad\nabla_{W^{(2)}}\mathcal L_n,n\nabla_{W^{(3)}}\mathcal L_n\bigr).
\end{gathered}
$$ {#eq-mfp-kernel-example-clock}

Relative to the full mean loss, the velocity is halved. The last-hidden-layer
feature kernel is $K_{n,ab}=h_a^{(2)T}h_b^{(2)}/n$; it is only the
readout block of the tangent kernel. For $r=0,1,2$ request

$$
J_r=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E\left[
\frac1{r!}\left.\frac{d^r}{dt^r}K_{n,12}(t)\right|_{t=0}\right].
$$ {#eq-mfp-kernel-example-jets}

Each coefficient exists by @thm-mfp-finite-derivative-program. For generic
$\phi$, form the loss gradient in the shared parameters, use the moving
recursion @eq-mfp-flow-jet-recursion through order two, and compile the
three scalar coefficients by @eq-mfp-source-response. All nonlinear
arguments in these differentiated initialization graphs are original
preactivations, so @prp-mfp-initialization-normal-form applies. The
zeroth coefficient is
$\mathbb E[\phi(Z_1)\phi(Z_2)]$ with
$Z\sim N(0,\Sigma^{(2)})$ from @eq-mfp-forward-covariances.
Higher generic formulas are finite expectation graphs and can be
regenerated by the maintained example; their expansion is not needed
to define or evaluate the algorithm.

For the compact linear check $\phi(z)=z$, the results are

$$
\begin{aligned}
J_0&=G_{12},\\
J_1&=0,\\
J_2&=\frac94(G_{11}y_1+G_{12}y_2)
                  (G_{12}y_1+G_{22}y_2).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-mfp-linear-kernel-jets}

Here is a direct derivation of the coefficient. Write
$W=W^{(2)}$, $w=W^{(3)}$, $v_b=W^{(1)}x_b/\sqrt d$,
$z_b=Wv_b$, $B=WW^T$ and
$s=\sum_c y_cv_c/m$. Put
$\lambda_b=\sum_cG_{bc}y_c/m$ and
$\rho=\sum_{c,e}y_cG_{ce}y_e/m^2$.
At initialization $f_{n,b}\to0$ in every finite $L^p$ because the
readout is centered and independent. Terms containing these scalar
predictions vanish in the expected finite jet limits: after expansion
their remaining normalized factors have all moments by the theorem.
Replacing residual values by $-y_c$ in the first velocity gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot W&=ws^T/n,\\
\dot w&=Ws,\\
\dot v_b&=\lambda_bW^Tw,\\
\dot z_b&=w k_b+\lambda_bBw,\\
k_b&=s^Tv_b/n\to\lambda_b.
\end{aligned}
$$

In the second derivative, retain the change of the residuals as well.
Their limiting derivatives are deterministic by the scalar theorem,
and multiply first feature derivatives that are odd in the centered
readout; their expected pairing with $z_b$ is zero. Replacing these
scalar residual derivatives by their limits is legitimate by Hölder
and the all-moment bounds. Thus they contribute zero to $J_2$.

For the remaining terms differentiate the displayed velocity. Since
$\dot s=\rho W^Tw$, one has
$\dot k_b=\rho w^Tz_b/n+\lambda_b w^TWs/n$, which tends to zero,
and
$\dot B=(w(Ws)^T+(Ws)w^T)/n$.
Conditioning on $W,v_1,v_2$ and using
$\mathbb E[ww^T]=I$ gives the following limiting pairings:

$$
\mathbb E\frac{\dot z_a^T\dot z_b}{n}\longrightarrow
5\lambda_a\lambda_b,\qquad
\mathbb E\frac{z_a^T\ddot z_b}{n}\longrightarrow
(1+1+2)\lambda_a\lambda_b=4\lambda_a\lambda_b.
$$

For clarity, the first coefficient is
$\lim\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}(I+B)^2/n=1+2+2=5$.
The three surviving terms in the second are respectively
$(Ws)k_b$, $\lambda_b(Ws)(w^Tw/n)$ and $\lambda_bBWs$.
The terms containing $w\dot k_b$ or $w((Ws)^Tw/n)$ vanish by
Cauchy--Schwarz and the $O(n^{-1})$ conditional second moments of the
normalized readout pairings. Gaussian pairings give
$\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}B/n=1$ and
$\mathbb E\operatorname{tr}B^2/n=2+1/n$; covariance of $v_a,s$ conditional on $W$ is $\lambda_a I$, yielding the stated cross-pairings.
For example, in $\operatorname{tr}B^2=
\sum_{i,j,k,l}W_{ik}W_{jk}W_{jl}W_{il}$ its three Gaussian pairings
contribute $n,n,1$. Consequently $K_{n,ab}''$ has limiting expectation
$(4+2\cdot5+4)\lambda_a\lambda_b=18\lambda_a\lambda_b$.
Dividing by $2!$ and putting $m=2$ proves @eq-mfp-linear-kernel-jets.
The first coefficient vanishes by readout centering after the same
residual-value replacement. These finite initial coefficients do not
reconstruct the feature kernel at positive time.

### Symbolic implementation {#sec-mfp-symbolic-interface}

The maintained interface is explicitly imported from
`pde.mfp_compiler`; it builds typed finite graphs, performs physical
differentiation, and returns @eq-mfp-expectation-graph. For example:

```python
from pde.mfp_compiler import Program

p = Program()
lower, upper = p.vector_type("lower"), p.vector_type("upper")
W = p.matrix("W", lower, upper)
z = W @ p.one(lower)
v = W.T @ p.phi(z)
answer = p.compile(p.inner(v, v), preactivations=[z])
print(answer.formula())
```

This returns the two activation moments in @eq-mfp-reuse-square.
`gradient` returns $n$ times vector gradients and ordinary matrix
gradients; `jets(..., moving=True)` returns factorial-normalized flow
coefficients. Supplying `preactivations` requests the restricted form
and checks its literal-node and Gaussian conditions. The caller still
supplies the architecture and activation-growth assumptions.

The [MFP API guide](../code/MFP_CALCULUS.md) gives executable reuse,
derivative and kernel-jet examples, supported operations and an independent
finite-array interpreter. The implementation uses exact rational
symbolic arithmetic; finite floats are converted by
`Fraction(str(value))`, and root covariances are concrete numeric inputs.
Symbolic geometry can instead enter through fixed scalar coefficients
such as $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ above. Generic integrals remain explicit;
the compiler performs no numerical quadrature. Higher derivatives and
expression expansion can grow rapidly. The theorem proves the limit
under its hypotheses; implementation tests check finite identities and
the emitted formulas.
